chapters.title: Chapter 2: Understanding the Asset Classes You're Trading

lessons.title: Currencies: USD-INR Futures and the Carry Trade Logic

body.text: A currency forward price is not the market's guess about where the exchange rate will be. It is almost entirely arithmetic, the interest rate gap between two currencies, and the carry trade is simply the bet that reality will look enough like that arithmetic for the gap to show up as profit rather than get erased by a sudden move in spot.

children.text: Currencies closed out Chapter 1's overview as the asset class every other asset class is priced in. This lesson goes deeper into USD-INR specifically: how the futures contract actually works on NSE, the interest rate parity logic that anchors its price, the carry trade this logic makes possible, and why the RBI's active management of the rupee makes USD-INR behave differently from a freely floating pair like EUR-USD.
How USD-INR Futures Actually Work on NSE

USD-INR futures on NSE are quoted in Indian rupees per US dollar, cash-settled against the RBI reference rate at expiry, with no physical delivery involved for standard contracts. Monthly expiries run out roughly a year ahead, which lets a systematic desk express a view or hold a hedge across a range of tenors without ever handling a foreign currency bank account. This is the instrument this course's currency signals, from here through Chapter 7's multi-strategy work, are built to trade.
Covered Interest Rate Parity: Why the Futures Price Isn't a Guess

Covered interest rate parity says the forward or futures exchange rate between two currencies is determined almost entirely by the interest rate differential between them, not by anyone's forecast of where spot will trade. If INR interest rates run higher than USD interest rates, the USD-INR futures price trades at a premium to spot, roughly in proportion to that rate gap and the time to expiry. This is arbitrage-enforced: if the futures price ever drifted far from what the rate differential implies, a trader could borrow in one currency, lend in the other, and lock in a risk-free profit, which competitive capital quickly closes.

children.text: The Carry Trade Logic: Getting Paid for the Rate Differential

When INR rates run higher than USD rates, a position that is effectively short USD and long INR earns the rate differential as carry, collected through the futures roll rather than a coupon or dividend. This is the same logic behind the classic global carry trade of borrowing in a low-yield currency to fund exposure to a higher-yield one, applied here to India specifically. The strategy works as long as the rupee does not depreciate against the dollar by more than the carry earned. It is a genuinely real, recurring return source, not free money, and Chapter 5 builds it into a full systematic strategy.

body.text: Carry trades are sometimes described as picking up nickels in front of a steamroller: small, steady gains most of the time, and an occasional large loss that can erase years of accumulated carry in weeks. During the 2013 taper tantrum, as the US Federal Reserve signaled winding down its bond-buying program, the rupee fell from around ₹54 to ₹55 per dollar in May 2013 to roughly ₹68 by August, over 20% in a few months, a move that would have devastated any unhedged INR carry position built on the assumption that the rupee would stay roughly range-bound.

children.text: RBI Isn't a Bystander: Managed Float, Not Free Float

markDefs.definition: An exchange rate regime where a currency is allowed to trade freely most of the time but where the central bank actively intervenes, buying or selling foreign currency, to smooth out volatility or resist moves it considers disorderly, without formally pegging the rate.

children.text: regime, not a fully free float like the US dollar against the euro. The RBI holds several hundred billion US dollars in foreign exchange reserves, among the largest reserve stockpiles of any central bank, and actively buys or sells dollars to smooth excessive volatility in either direction. This has a direct modeling consequence: USD-INR's realized volatility tends to run structurally lower than a comparable freely floating emerging-market currency in calm periods, since RBI intervention dampens smaller moves, but this can make sharp moves, on the rare occasions the RBI steps back or is overwhelmed by flow, feel disproportionately sudden relative to the calm that preceded them.

children.text: What Drives USD-INR Day to Day

Beyond the interest rate differential that anchors the futures price, day-to-day spot moves are driven by FII and FDI flows in and out of Indian markets, the current account and trade deficit, with crude oil imports a major swing factor as covered in the previous lesson, RBI reserve intervention, and the broader strength or weakness of the US dollar globally, often tracked through the Dollar Index, DXY.

columns.label: Drivers That Push INR Weaker

Widening trade deficit, often crude-price driven
Broad US dollar strength globally (rising DXY)

columns.label: Drivers That Push INR Stronger
points: FII and FDI inflows into Indian markets
Narrowing trade deficit, often from falling crude prices
Broad US dollar weakness globally (falling DXY)
RBI actively defending the rupee via reserve sales

children.text: Currency as Both a Standalone Asset and a Hidden Exposure

Chapter 1 already flagged that unhedged foreign exposure, a US equity fund, gold priced in dollars, is implicitly a currency bet layered on top of whatever asset class it appears to be. This lesson's point is the flip side: currencies are also a standalone, tradable asset class with their own return driver, interest rate differentials, expressed cleanly through USD-INR futures. A multi-asset systematic book needs an explicit, deliberate policy on both fronts, whether to run currency exposure as its own signal, and whether to hedge the currency risk that rides along inside every other cross-border position.

body.title: The Carry Trade That Worked, Until It Didn't
body.scenario: A systematic desk runs a currency carry strategy through 2012 and into mid-2013: short USD, long INR, collecting the rate differential steadily via the futures roll every month, with returns matching the model's expectations almost exactly. In May 2013, the strategy is still fully positioned when the US Federal Reserve signals it will begin tapering its bond-buying program.
body.prompt: Using what this lesson covered, explain what happened to this position over the following months, and what kind of risk management would have limited the damage.
body.modelAnswer: The rupee depreciated sharply against the dollar through the 2013 taper tantrum, falling from around ₹54 to ₹55 to roughly ₹68 over a few months, as FII outflows accelerated and the market repriced Fed policy expectations. A short USD, long INR carry position loses money directly when the rupee weakens, and a move of this size would have wiped out a large multiple of whatever carry the position had earned over the prior year. Risk management that would have limited the damage includes position sizing that assumes carry trades carry meaningful tail risk rather than steady, low-volatility income, and a drawdown-based stop or volatility trigger that reduces or exits the position once realized currency volatility spikes well above its recent calm-period range, rather than waiting for a full stop-loss level to be hit.

body.title: Applying Covered Interest Rate Parity
body.prompt: Spot USD-INR is ₹83.00. The 1-year INR interest rate is 6.5% and the 1-year USD interest rate is 5.0%. Using F ≈ S × (1 + (r_INR - r_USD) × T) with T = 1, what is the approximate 1-year forward USD-INR rate? Round to two decimal places.
body.explanation: F ≈ 83.00 × (1 + 0.015 × 1) = 83.00 × 1.015 = 84.245, which rounds to approximately ₹84.25. The roughly ₹1.25 premium reflects the 1.5 percentage point rate gap between INR and USD, not a market forecast of rupee depreciation.

body.title: Managed Float, Applied
body.question: What is the main practical consequence for a systematic desk of USD-INR trading under a managed float rather than a free float?
options: USD-INR cannot be traded systematically at all under a managed float
Realized volatility tends to run structurally lower in calm periods due to RBI intervention, which can make the rare sharp move feel disproportionately sudden
The RBI sets USD-INR at a fixed, unchanging rate
Covered interest rate parity no longer applies to USD-INR
body.explanation: A managed float means the RBI actively smooths volatility rather than letting USD-INR move entirely freely, which tends to suppress realized volatility in calm periods while making the occasional large move, when intervention steps back or is overwhelmed, feel sharper by comparison. Covered interest rate parity still applies; it governs the futures-to-spot relationship regardless of how actively the central bank manages spot volatility.

points: USD-INR futures on NSE are cash-settled against the RBI reference rate, quoted in rupees per dollar, with expiries out to about a year
Covered interest rate parity anchors the futures price to the INR-USD interest rate differential, not to a forecast of where spot will move

The currency carry trade earns that rate differential through the futures roll, but is exposed to sharp rupee depreciation that can erase years of accumulated carry, as the 2013 taper tantrum demonstrated

The rupee trades under a managed float, with the RBI actively intervening using substantial foreign exchange reserves, which suppresses calm-period volatility but can make rare sharp moves feel sudden
USD-INR's day-to-day drivers include FII and FDI flows, the trade deficit (crude-sensitive), RBI intervention, and broad global dollar strength
A multi-asset book needs an explicit currency policy covering both currency as a standalone tradable asset and the hidden currency exposure riding inside foreign or dollar-priced positions
